what: SiteOne is the largest wholesale distributor of landscaping supplies in the United States and Canada. It sells irrigation equipment, plants, fertiliser, pavers, stone, outdoor lighting and tools through more than 600 branches, and has grown by buying dozens of small local distributors.
customers: Professional landscape contractors who build and maintain lawns, gardens and outdoor spaces for homes, businesses and municipalities.
money: Fertiliser, irrigation parts and tools that contractors use every season.
Materials for landscaping new homes and commercial projects.
moat: Scale in a fragmented market: SiteOne is several times larger than its nearest competitor and can offer contractors one-stop shopping, credit and local stock. Each acquisition adds branches it can supply more cheaply.
risks: Net income fell from $245M in 2022 to $124M in 2024 as prices for commodity products such as fertiliser and PVC pipe came down, and recovered only to $152M in 2025.
New home construction is weak, which hits the construction side.
Growth by acquisition can hide weak organic growth.
At 28 times trailing earnings, the price assumes margins rebuild.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $3.48B in 2021 to $4.71B in 2025.
More than half of sales comes from maintenance, which continues regardless of housing starts.
Free cash flow of about $250M a year funds acquisitions without much borrowing.
There are still thousands of small distributors left to buy.
watch: Organic daily sales growth and gross margin, which show whether pricing pressure has passed.
view: SiteOne is a classic roll-up of a fragmented trade, and it has executed well: revenue up every year, from $3.5 billion to $4.7 billion since 2021, funded largely from its own cash flow. What has gone wrong is profit. Net income halved from 2022 to 2024 as commodity prices fell and price increases reversed, and the recovery since has been slow.

The market is paying 28 times trailing earnings, which only makes sense if margins return toward their 2021–2022 level. I think that is partly cyclical: weak new housing has hurt the construction side, and maintenance demand has held up. But part of the 2021–2022 margin was inflation windfall that should not be expected again.

This is a high-quality business at a full price. I would not chase it here; the time to buy roll-ups like this is when housing is at its worst and the shares are out of favour. At today’s valuation you are paying for a recovery that has not yet shown up in the numbers.
bull: Housing recovers, commodity prices stabilise and margins rebuild, with acquisitions adding growth on top.
bear: Margins stay below their peak and the 28 times multiple contracts.
